name: The Copper Beech of Schoonoord
access: Free, daily 8:30-16:30 (closes during large festivals in adjoining Het Park)
transport: Walkable from central Rotterdam, near the Euromast, roughly 15 minutes
verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1696614) gives a detailed history: planted at the original layout of Schoonoord garden between 1860 and 1870, one of the oldest surviving 'carriers' of the garden alongside the two Lebanon cedars. Register text: trunk 'dikke stam van 125 cm', height approx 20m, crown width approx 18m; unclear whether the 125cm figure is diameter or girth (Dutch 'dik'/'dikte' usually means thickness/diameter, which would put circumference near 390cm for a tree this age -- record with that caveat, do not treat 125 as a confirmed girth_cm). Wikipedia separately mentions 'a 200-year-old beech' among the park's notable trees without naming it as the copper beech specifically; that figure conflicts with the register's 1860-1870 planting band (roughly 155-165 years as of 2026) and may refer to a different beech or be a rounded/unverified figure repeated by tourism copy. Flagged for that age conflict; register age used as primary since it is the most specific per-tree source. Schoonoord is a former country estate (buitenplaats), a protected Rijksmonument since 2000, 1.2 hectares, owned by Stichting Schoonoord and managed by the municipality of Rotterdam; opened to the public in 1973. Stands beside a pond along a narrow footpath near the Westzeedijk boundary of the garden. Surrounded by roughly 1000 other plant and tree species; the garden also holds bee colonies, koi in the pond, a tawny owl and kingfishers. Register: owner_category stichting, visitable ja, visible nee (not visible from outside the garden, entry required).

name: The Lebanon Cedars of Schoonoord
age_estimate: roughly 155-165 years (register); local sources say over 250 years
access: Free, daily 8:30-16:30 (closes during large festivals in adjoining Het Park)
transport: Walkable from central Rotterdam, near the Euromast, roughly 15 minutes
verify_notes: Register entry (LRMB nr 1694861) covers a pair of Cedars of Lebanon standing together at one point in the garden (n_trees: 2), the same 'gigantic Libanonceders' both the official garden site and Wikipedia call the garden's best-known trees; treated as one ensemble entry since a visitor sees them as one feature at one obvious spot. AGE CONFLICT, not resolved: the register's own history text places them at the garden's original 1860s planting (roughly 155-165 years as of 2026), while Wikipedia and multiple tourism write-ups describe them as 'ruim 250 jaar oud' (over 250 years old), which would predate the garden's 1860 layout entirely and may instead describe cedars transplanted as older specimens, or may simply be an unverified figure repeated across sites. Neither figure can be preferred with confidence; both are recorded, flagged, and left for the writer to state as a disputed age rather than pick one. Same Rijksmonument garden as the copper beech (rot_010): free access, owned by Stichting Schoonoord, managed by the municipality, opened to the public in 1973. Register: owner_category stichting, visitable ja, visible nee.

name: The Atlas Cedar of Heemraadspark

location.address: Heemraadssingel, near the Schietbaanbrug, west side near no. 215B, Rotterdam

access: Free, public canalside park (Heemraadssingel/Heemraadspark), open at any time
transport: Walkable from central Rotterdam, Nieuwe Westen district, roughly 20-25 minutes; also reachable by tram along the singel
verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1695437) gives a simple history: 'Geplant in 1930', planted band 1930-1940, on municipal land (owner_category gemeente) beside the Heemraadssingel canal near the Schietbaanbrug footbridge (a wooden bridge from 1867, itself a municipal monument), west side near house number 215B. Rotterdam's own official monumental-trees page (rotterdam.nl/monumentale-bomen) separately lists a 'Heemraadssingel Cedar, 100+ years old', which is the same feature though its age estimate (100+ years, implying a pre-1926 planting) runs a little ahead of the register's 1930-1940 band; flagged for that minor conflict, register age used as primary since it names an exact planting year. A general web search also found a secondary description (via monumentaltrees.com, not fetched directly and not used as a source per hard rule 1) of 'two Atlas cedars' grouped near Schietbaanlaan around house number 180, consistent with more than one cedar standing along this stretch of the singel; this entry covers the specific tree at the register's own coordinate. Heemraadssingel is one of Rotterdam's oldest and best-preserved canals (laid out c.1900-1915, protected cityscape, roughly fifty tree species along it, planes and lindens dominant). Register: visitable ja, visible ja.
